description: Barina's verification project distributes work across European supercomputers in units of 2^40 consecutive integers. Each work unit takes ~10 seconds on a modern GPU. Angeltveit's algorithm instead shards by the last k bits (55, 1168, or 278699 cases of similar running time), which is inherently non-sequential but enables better load balancing. Both approaches face the classic distributed computing challenge of fault tolerance and progress tracking.
mathematical_formalization: Barina: partition [1, 2^N] into intervals [i*2^40, (i+1)*2^40) for i = 0,...,2^{N-40}-1. Angeltveit: partition by residue classes mod 2^k, yielding C(k) ≈ 0.08% * 2^k cases, each with ~2^{N-k}/C(k) effective integers to check. Load balance: Var(T_i) / E[T_i]^2 measures uniformity.
analogical_connections: MapReduce shuffling — partition data by key for balanced reducer loads
BOINC volunteer computing — distribute independent work units with checkpointing
Consistent hashing in distributed databases — shard by hash for uniform distribution
implementation_hypothesis: Implement a work-unit server (like Barina's pcbarina.fit.vutbr.cz) that tracks completion status. For Angeltveit-style sharding, precompute the ~278699 cases on the coordinator, assign batches to GPU workers. Workers report back a checksum (hash of all path records found). Coordinator validates checksums against CPU-computed reference for a random sample.
experiment_seed: Simulate both sharding strategies for N=72 with heterogeneous GPU fleet (mix of RTX 3060, 4090, A100). Measure: makespan, load imbalance factor, network overhead. Test a hybrid approach: Angeltveit sharding for the recursive phase, Barina-style intervals for Step 3 residuals.
